Lab 7: Nested Data

Intermediate Quantitative Methods · Week 7

Author

Sebastian Ramirez-Ruiz

Term

Autumn 2026

Welcome! 👋

This week’s seminar was about nested data: weeks within legislators, legislators within parties, parties within countries. We split the error term into parts, a legislator’s stable traits (\(\nu_i\)), the week everyone shares (\(\theta_t\)), and everything else, and asked what to do with them. Today we follow the same arc in R, with the same simulated legislators on TikTok. The lab has three parts, plus an optional fourth:

  • First, what hides in the error term: the two simple comparisons from the seminar, how nested the data are, and what ignoring it does to standard errors.
  • Second, remove it: fixed effects, the 2×2 difference-in-differences table by hand, and two-way fixed effects.
  • Third, model it: partial pooling, the random-effects model, and the within-between model.
  • Fourth, optional and on your own: cross-level interactions and random slopes. Martín will not cover this part in the lab.

Along the way, we add a few R tools: group-wise operations with dplyr::mutate(.by = ), fixed effects with {fixest}, multilevel models with {lme4}, clustered standard errors, and side-by-side tables with {modelsummary}.

As in the last labs, the data are simulated, so we know the truth and can check whether each model recovers it.

Plan for today ≈ time
What hides in the error term: two comparisons, the ICC, clustered standard errors 30 min
Remove it: fixed effects, the 2×2 table, two-way fixed effects 35 min
Model it: pooling, random effects, the within-between model 40 min
Wrap-up 10 min

Packages 📦

# Install these in your CONSOLE if you have not done so yet:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "modelsummary", "broom.mixed", "fixest", "lme4",
#                    "estimatr", "clubSandwich", "marginaleffects"))

library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plots; loads {dplyr}, {tidyr}, {purrr}, {ggplot2}

We call the other packages with package::function(), so you always see where a function comes from: {modelsummary} for tables (it needs {broom.mixed} installed to read multilevel models), {fixest} for fixed effects, {lme4} for multilevel models, {estimatr} and {clubSandwich} for clustered standard errors, and {marginaleffects} for predictions.

The legislators on TikTok 🎬

Every TikTok video posted by legislators of every party in 12 countries, over the 40 weeks before an election. A classifier gives each video a criticism score, from 0 to 100: how critical it is, of opponents, the government, or even the legislator’s own party. Our outcome is a legislator’s average score in a week; weeks without videos are missing.

Along the way, some legislators announce they will not run again: they become lame ducks, each at their own time. Do they find their critical voice? In the simulation, yes: becoming a lame duck raises criticism by 5 points. Three more things are built in, as in the seminar:

  • Senior legislators are calmer online, and much more likely to retire. Seniority is part of \(\nu_i\).
  • The campaign heats up everyone’s feed in the last 16 weeks (\(\theta_t\)), and most announcements come just before it.
  • Frontbenchers post every week; many backbenchers post only now and then.

The function below builds this world. It is the same code, and the same seed, as in the seminar, so you get the same numbers:

make_world <- function(seed = 3, het = 0) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n_c <- 12
  countries <- tibble::tibble(country = paste("Country", LETTERS[1:n_c]),
                              polarization = as.vector(scale(rnorm(n_c))),
                              c_eff = 3 * polarization + rnorm(n_c, 0, 2))
  parties <- countries %>%
    tidyr::uncount(6, .id = "p") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(party = paste0(country, "-", p), populist = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, 0.3),
                  p_eff = 8 * populist + rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 3),
                  size = round(exp(runif(dplyr::n(), log(3), log(30)))))
  legislators <- parties %>%
    tidyr::uncount(size, .id = "l") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(legislator = paste0(party, "-", l), senior = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, 0.3),
                  l_eff = -13 * senior + rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 5),
                  retires = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, plogis(-2.6 + 3 * senior)),
                  announce = ifelse(retires == 1, sample(12:36, dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE, prob = (12:36)^2), NA),
                  front = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, 0.3),
                  rate = ifelse(front == 1, 3, runif(dplyr::n(), 0.05, 0.8)))
  theta <- c(rep(0, 24), 1:12, rep(12, 4)) # the campaign: weeks 25-40
  legislators %>%
    tidyr::expand_grid(week = 1:40) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(videos = rpois(dplyr::n(), rate)) %>%
    dplyr::filter(videos > 0) %>%                       # weeks without videos are missing
    dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() >= 2, .by = legislator) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(lame_duck = as.integer(!is.na(announce) & week >= announce),
                  latent = 30 + (5 + het * polarization) * lame_duck + c_eff + p_eff + l_eff +
                    theta[week] + rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 4),
                  criticism = pmin(pmax(latent + rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 15) / sqrt(videos), 0), 100)) %>%
    dplyr::select(country, polarization, party, populist, legislator, senior, front, retires,
                  announce, week, videos, lame_duck, criticism)
}

pan <- make_world()
dplyr::glimpse(pan)
Rows: 18,771

One row per legislator-week. lame_duck switches on in the week a legislator announces (announce) and stays on; retires marks the legislators who will announce at some point. senior is in the data so that we can check our answers: in real data, it would be one of the many stable traits we do not measure.

pan %>%
  dplyr::summarize(countries = dplyr::n_distinct(country),
                   parties = dplyr::n_distinct(party),
                   legislators = dplyr::n_distinct(legislator),
                   lame_ducks = dplyr::n_distinct(legislator[retires == 1]),
                   legislator_weeks = dplyr::n())

Part I: What hides in the error term 🔍

The criticism of legislator \(i\) in week \(t\) has parts:

\[Y_{it} = \beta D_{it} + \underbrace{\nu_i + \theta_t + \eta_{it}}_{\varepsilon_{it}}\]

where \(\nu_i\) is what the legislator brings every week (seniority, style, party, country), \(\theta_t\) what the week brings everyone (the campaign), and \(\eta_{it}\) everything else.

Two comparisons ⚖️

The seminar started with two simple comparisons. Each is a regression on a slice of the data:

after_only <- pan %>% dplyr::filter(week >= 37)              # after every announcement
lame_ducks_only <- pan %>% dplyr::filter(retires == 1,       # lame ducks only,
                                         week <= 11 | week >= 37) # before and after

comparisons <- list(
  "Lame ducks vs. run again, after" = lm(criticism ~ lame_duck, data = after_only),
  "Lame ducks, before vs. after" = lm(criticism ~ lame_duck, data = lame_ducks_only)
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(comparisons,
                           coef_map = c("lame_duck" = "Lame duck"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
Lame ducks vs. run again, after Lame ducks, before vs. after
Lame duck -2.994 16.660
(0.808) (0.832)
Num.Obs. 1881 1620

Activity 💡

The truth is +5. For each comparison: is it too small, too large, or the wrong sign? Which part of the error term, \(\nu_i\) or \(\theta_t\), cancels, and which one is still in it?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓
  • Lame ducks vs. those who run again, after (about −3): the wrong sign. Same weeks, so \(\theta_t\) cancels. But lame ducks are mostly seniors, who are calmer anyway: \(\nu_i\) is still in it.
  • Lame ducks, before vs. after (about +17): far too large. Same people, so \(\nu_i\) cancels. But the campaign heats up everyone’s feed in between: \(\theta_t\) is still in it.

How nested are the data? 🪆

A legislator’s weeks share \(\nu_i\): a combative legislator is combative every week. The intraclass correlation (ICC) says how much of the variance in criticism lies between legislators rather than within them, \(\tau^2 / (\tau^2 + \sigma^2)\). A random-intercept model with no predictors estimates both variances. In {lme4}, (1 | legislator) means “one intercept per legislator, drawn from a common distribution”:

m0 <- lme4::lmer(criticism ~ 1 + (1 | legislator), data = pan)

vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(m0))
vc
vc$vcov[1] / sum(vc$vcov) # the ICC
[1] 0.3246547

About a third of the variance is between legislators. Two weeks of the same legislator are much more alike than two random legislator-weeks.

What ignoring it does to standard errors 📏

Do legislators in more polarized countries post more critical videos? Polarization is a country-level variable: it takes 12 values. A plain regression treats every legislator-week as an independent piece of evidence. estimatr::lm_robust(..., clusters = country) fits the same regression but clusters the standard errors by country, so the evidence on polarization counts countries, not rows:

polarization_models <- list(
  "lm()" = lm(criticism ~ polarization, data = pan),
  "lm_robust(clusters = country)" = estimatr::lm_robust(criticism ~ polarization, data = pan, clusters = country)
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(polarization_models,
                           coef_map = c("polarization" = "Polarization (+1 SD)"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
lm() lm_robust(clusters = country)
Polarization (+1 SD) 3.521 3.521
(0.117) (1.056)
Num.Obs. 18771 18771

Same estimate, a much larger standard error. Which one should we believe? This function simulates a world where a country-level variable z has no effect at all, and returns the p-value for z from both regressions:

sim_null <- function(n_countries = 12, n_per = 300) {
  d <- tibble::tibble(country = rep(1:n_countries, each = n_per),
                      z = rep(rnorm(n_countries), each = n_per),          # no effect on y
                      u = rep(rnorm(n_countries, 0, 4), each = n_per)) %>% # country effect
    dplyr::mutate(y = 30 + u + rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 12))
  tibble::tibble(naive = summary(lm(y ~ z, data = d))$coefficients["z", 4],
                 clustered = estimatr::lm_robust(y ~ z, data = d, clusters = country)$p.value[["z"]])
}

sim_null()

Activity 💡

Run sim_null() 200 times (purrr::map() and purrr::list_rbind(), as in earlier labs) and compute how often each p-value is below 0.05. How often should it be?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
set.seed(70)
sims <- purrr::map(1:200, \(i) sim_null()) %>% purrr::list_rbind()

sims %>% dplyr::summarize(naive = mean(naive < 0.05), clustered = mean(clustered < 0.05))

It should be 5%: z has no effect, so a test at the 5% level should reject 5% of the time. The naive p-values reject most of the time: they treat thousands of rows as the evidence for a 12-country claim. The clustered ones are close to 5% (with 200 runs, anything between about 2% and 8% is simulation noise). Cluster the standard errors at the level where the variable, or the treatment, varies.

Part II: Remove it: fixed effects ✂️

Compare each legislator with themselves 🪞

Unit fixed effects compare each legislator with themselves, so anything constant within a legislator, like \(\nu_i\), drops out. Three ways to do it, one answer, next to pooled OLS:

# demeaning by hand: subtract each legislator's own average
pan_dm <- pan %>%
  dplyr::mutate(crit_dm = criticism - mean(criticism),
                ld_dm = lame_duck - mean(lame_duck),
                .by = legislator) # .by: the mean within each legislator

fe_models <- list(
  "Pooled OLS" = lm(criticism ~ lame_duck, data = pan),
  "A dummy per legislator" = lm(criticism ~ lame_duck + factor(legislator), data = pan),
  "Demeaned by hand" = lm(crit_dm ~ ld_dm, data = pan_dm),
  "fixest::feols()" = fixest::feols(criticism ~ lame_duck | legislator, cluster = ~legislator, data = pan)
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(fe_models,
                           coef_map = c("lame_duck" = "Lame duck", "ld_dm" = "Lame duck"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
Pooled OLS A dummy per legislator Demeaned by hand fixest::feols()
Lame duck 4.122 13.249 13.249 13.249
(0.446) (0.451) (0.440) (0.501)
Num.Obs. 18771 18771 18771 18771

Pooled OLS is too small: it mixes the lame ducks’ new voice with who they are. The three fixed-effects estimates agree, and are far too large. That is not a bug: comparing lame ducks with themselves, the campaign is added to their new voice. Look at the legislators who never retire, week by week:

pan %>%
  dplyr::filter(retires == 0) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(criticism = mean(criticism), .by = week) %>%
  ggplot(aes(week, criticism)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 24.5, xmax = 40.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#f6f0e4") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "#1d375b") +
  labs(x = "Week (campaign shaded)", y = "Average criticism, legislators who run again") +
  theme_minimal()

Both comparisons at once: the 2×2 table 🧮

Keep the weeks before anyone announces (1–11) and the weeks after every announcement (37–40):

pan_2x2 <- pan %>%
  dplyr::filter(week <= 11 | week >= 37) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(after = as.integer(week >= 37))

Activity 💡

  1. Compute the average criticism in the four cells: lame ducks (retires == 1) and those who run again, before and after. Hint: dplyr::summarize(..., .by = c(retires, after)).
  2. Compute the difference in differences: the lame ducks’ change (after − before) minus the change of those who run again. Then check it against the interaction in lm(criticism ~ retires * after, data = pan_2x2).
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
cells <- pan_2x2 %>%
  dplyr::summarize(criticism = mean(criticism), .by = c(retires, after))
cells
# 2.
y <- function(r, a) cells$criticism[cells$retires == r & cells$after == a]
(y(1, 1) - y(1, 0)) - (y(0, 1) - y(0, 0))
[1] 4.967283
modelsummary::modelsummary(lm(criticism ~ retires * after, data = pan_2x2),
                           coef_map = c("retires:after" = "Retires × after"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
(1)
Retires × after 4.967
(0.946)
Num.Obs. 7085
  1. Before, future lame ducks are already much calmer than those who run again (mostly seniors). After, both groups are more critical (the campaign).
  2. About +5. Subtracting the change of those who run again removes the campaign (\(\theta_t\)); comparing each group with itself removes who they are (\(\nu_i\)). The interaction coefficient is exactly the difference in differences.

Two-way fixed effects ⚖️

With staggered announcements there is no single “before” and “after”. Two-way fixed effects do the same subtraction for every legislator and every week at once: legislator fixed effects remove \(\nu_i\), week fixed effects remove \(\theta_t\). We cluster the standard errors by legislator, the level at which the treatment is assigned (ask for it explicitly: depending on the version, {fixest} reports iid standard errors by default):

fit_twfe <- fixest::feols(criticism ~ lame_duck | legislator + week, cluster = ~legislator, data = pan)

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Pooled OLS" = fe_models[["Pooled OLS"]],
       "Legislator FE" = fe_models[["fixest::feols()"]],
       "Legislator + week FE" = fit_twfe),
  coef_map = c("lame_duck" = "Lame duck"),
  gof_map = "nobs"
)
Pooled OLS Legislator FE Legislator + week FE
Lame duck 4.122 13.249 5.116
(0.446) (0.501) (0.476)
Num.Obs. 18771 18771 18771

Close to 5.

populist is removed for collinearity: it is constant within each legislator, so the legislator fixed effects absorb it. Unit fixed effects remove every stable variable, including the ones we would like to study.

Part III: Model it: random effects and the within-between model 🧩

Complete, no, and partial pooling 🫗

How critical is legislator \(i\), on average? Three models, three answers:

  • Complete pooling, lm(criticism ~ 1): one average for everyone.
  • No pooling, lm(criticism ~ 0 + legislator): one average per legislator, each from its own weeks only.
  • Partial pooling, lme4::lmer(criticism ~ 1 + (1 | legislator)): one intercept per legislator, drawn from a common distribution. That is m0, from Part I.
complete <- mean(pan$criticism)

no_pool <- pan %>% # the same numbers as lm(criticism ~ 0 + legislator), but faster
  dplyr::summarize(own = mean(criticism), n_weeks = dplyr::n(), .by = legislator)

partial <- coef(m0)$legislator %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("legislator") %>%
  dplyr::rename(partial = `(Intercept)`)

pooling <- no_pool %>% dplyr::left_join(partial, by = "legislator")

ggplot(pooling, aes(n_weeks)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = complete, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888888") +
  geom_segment(aes(y = own, yend = partial, xend = n_weeks), color = "#639E7D",
               arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(5, "pt")), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = own), color = "#6B8CB8", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Weeks in which the legislator posted (log scale)", y = "Average criticism",
       caption = "Blue: each legislator's own average. Arrowheads: partial pooling. Dashed: complete pooling.") +
  theme_minimal()

The partial-pooling estimate is a weighted average of the legislator’s own average and the overall mean. The weight on their own data, \(n_i\tau^2 / (n_i\tau^2 + \sigma^2)\), grows with the number of weeks we see them, \(n_i\). This is shrinkage.

Activity 💡

Find a legislator seen in only 2 weeks and one seen in all 40 (dplyr::filter(pooling, n_weeks %in% c(2, 40))). For each, compare their own average with the partial-pooling estimate. Which one moved more toward the overall mean, and why?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
pooling %>%
  dplyr::filter(n_weeks %in% c(2, 40)) %>%
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1, by = n_weeks) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(moved = partial - own)

The legislator seen in 2 weeks moves much more: two weeks are a noisy average, so the model trusts it less and pulls it toward the overall mean. Forty weeks are a precise average, and it barely moves.

Random effects, and the within-between model 🔀

Add the treatment and the week effects to the partial-pooling model, and we have the random-effects model. Its catch: it assumes \(\nu_i\) is unrelated to the treatment, which fails here (seniors are calmer and more likely to retire). The within-between model fixes it by splitting the treatment into each legislator’s average and their deviation from it. Hazlett & Wainstein’s bias-corrected version keeps the treatment as it is and adds the average; with cluster-robust standard errors from {clubSandwich}, it lines up with two-way fixed effects:

pan <- pan %>%
  dplyr::mutate(d_mean = mean(lame_duck),    # between: the legislator's average
                d_dev = lame_duck - d_mean,   # within: the deviation from it
                .by = legislator)

m_re <- lme4::lmer(criticism ~ lame_duck + factor(week) + (1 | legislator), data = pan)
m_wb <- lme4::lmer(criticism ~ d_dev + d_mean + factor(week) + (1 | legislator), data = pan)
m_bc <- lme4::lmer(criticism ~ lame_duck + d_mean + factor(week) + (1 | legislator), data = pan)

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Two-way FE" = fit_twfe,
       "Random effects" = m_re,
       "Within-between" = m_wb,
       "Bias-corrected" = m_bc),
  vcov = list(NULL, NULL, NULL, as.matrix(clubSandwich::vcovCR(m_bc, type = "CR2"))),
  coef_map = c("lame_duck" = "Lame duck", "d_dev" = "Lame duck (within)",
               "d_mean" = "Share of weeks as lame duck (between)"),
  gof_map = "nobs",
  notes = "Standard errors: clustered by legislator (two-way FE), model-based (random effects, within-between), cluster-robust CR2 (bias-corrected)."
)
Two-way FE Random effects Within-between Bias-corrected
Standard errors: clustered by legislator (two-way FE), model-based (random effects, within-between), cluster-robust CR2 (bias-corrected).
Lame duck 5.116 4.342 5.109
(0.476) (0.453) (0.477)
Lame duck (within) 5.109
(0.465)
Share of weeks as lame duck (between) -9.040 -14.149
(1.870) (2.246)
Num.Obs. 18771 18771 18771 18771

A word on the lingo: in multilevel modeling, the “fixed effects” are the coefficients that are the same for everyone (what lme4::fixef() returns), and the “random effects” are the \(\nu_i\). These are not the legislator fixed effects of Part II.

Activity 💡

  1. Which estimates are close to the truth (+5)? Why is the plain random-effects model off?
  2. In real data, seniority would be unobserved. Here it is in the data: add senior to the within-between model m_wb. What happens to the within and the between coefficients?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 2.
m_wb_senior <- lme4::lmer(criticism ~ d_dev + d_mean + senior + factor(week) + (1 | legislator), data = pan)

modelsummary::modelsummary(list("Within-between" = m_wb, "+ seniority" = m_wb_senior),
                           coef_map = c("d_dev" = "Within", "d_mean" = "Between", "senior" = "Senior"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
Within-between + seniority
Within 5.109 5.122
(0.465) (0.465)
Between -9.040 6.031
(1.870) (1.858)
Senior -11.901
(0.695)
Num.Obs. 18771 18771
  1. Two-way FE, the within coefficient, and the bias-corrected model are all close to 5, with practically the same standard error once the bias-corrected model’s is cluster-robust. The plain random-effects model is lower: it blends the within comparison with the between one, and between legislators, the lame ducks are calmer (seniors).
  2. The within coefficient does not move: it never depended on seniority, which is constant within a legislator. The between coefficient flips sign: once seniority is held constant, legislators who spend more of the period as lame ducks are more critical. The negative between coefficient was mostly about seniority, and in real data, most stable confounders are unmeasured.

One model, three questions 🎯

What multilevel models add: we can keep the within effect and ask about stable variables at their own level, populism (party) and polarization (country). The truths in the simulation are 5, 8, and 3:

m_ml <- lme4::lmer(
  criticism ~ d_dev + d_mean +
    populist + polarization +
    factor(week) +
    (1 | country/party/legislator),
  data = pan
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(m_ml,
                           coef_map = c("d_dev" = "Lame duck (within)", "populist" = "Populist party",
                                        "polarization" = "Polarization (+1 SD)"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
(1)
Lame duck (within) 5.098
(0.465)
Populist party 7.388
(0.865)
Polarization (+1 SD) 3.422
(0.701)
Num.Obs. 18771

All three land near their truths here, but polarization rests on 12 countries, and its standard error is the largest relative to its estimate.

Predictions need one more choice: for whom? re.form = NA sets \(\nu_i = 0\), a typical legislator; without it, the prediction uses a known legislator’s own (shrunken) \(\nu_i\):

marginaleffects::predictions(m_re,
  newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(legislator = "Country A-1-1", lame_duck = 0:1, week = 30))

    legislator lame_duck week Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 %

 Country A-1-1         1   30     34.1      0.759 44.9   <0.001 Inf  32.6

Type: response
marginaleffects::predictions(m_re,
  newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(lame_duck = 0:1, week = 30), re.form = NA)

 lame_duck week Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %

The levels differ, the gap does not: the model has one lame-duck effect for everyone.

Part IV (optional): Cross-level interactions and random slopes 🌐

⚠️ This part is optional, for you to work through on your own if you are interested. Martín will not cover it in the lab. It follows the auxiliary slides on multilevel models in practice, and Bell, Fairbrother & Jones (2019), the compulsory reading.

Does polarization change the lame-duck effect? 🌡

A new world, from the same function: now the lame-duck effect grows with polarization, \(5 + 2 \times \text{polarization}\). Does a country feature change a legislator-level relationship? That is a cross-level interaction. First, the effect estimated separately in each country:

pan_x <- make_world(het = 2)

by_country <- pan_x %>%
  dplyr::filter(sum(retires) > 0, .by = country) %>%
  tidyr::nest(.by = c(country, polarization)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(effect = purrr::map_dbl(data, \(d) {
    coef(fixest::feols(criticism ~ lame_duck | legislator + week, data = d))[["lame_duck"]]
  }))

ggplot(by_country, aes(polarization, effect)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#c6273b") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1d375b") +
  labs(x = "Polarization (standardized)", y = "Lame-duck effect within the country") +
  theme_minimal()

In one multilevel model, the interaction lame_duck * polarization asks the same question. The random slope (1 + lame_duck | country) lets the lame-duck effect differ from country to country beyond what polarization explains:

m_x <- lme4::lmer(criticism ~ lame_duck * polarization + factor(week) +
                    (1 | legislator) + (1 + lame_duck | country), data = pan_x)

modelsummary::modelsummary(m_x,
                           coef_map = c("lame_duck" = "Lame duck", "lame_duck:polarization" = "Lame duck × polarization"),
                           gof_map = "nobs")
(1)
Lame duck 4.185
(0.531)
Lame duck × polarization 1.869
(0.530)
Num.Obs. 18771

Close to the truth of 2. But what if polarization changed nothing? This function simulates such a world (the effect differs across 12 countries, but not with polarization), fits the interaction with and without the random slope, and records whether each calls it “significant”:

sim_slopes <- function(n_countries = 12, n_per = 400) {
  d <- tibble::tibble(country = 1:n_countries, polarization = rnorm(n_countries),
                      u0 = rnorm(n_countries, 0, 3), u1 = rnorm(n_countries, 0, 2)) %>%
    dplyr::slice(rep(1:n_countries, each = n_per)) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(lame_duck = rbinom(dplyr::n(), 1, 0.5),
                  y = 30 + u0 + (5 + u1) * lame_duck + rnorm(dplyr::n(), 0, 10))
  t_ri <- summary(lme4::lmer(y ~ lame_duck * polarization + (1 | country), data = d))$coefficients["lame_duck:polarization", "t value"]
  t_rs <- summary(lme4::lmer(y ~ lame_duck * polarization + (1 + lame_duck | country), data = d))$coefficients["lame_duck:polarization", "t value"]
  tibble::tibble(intercept_only = abs(t_ri) > 1.96, random_slope = abs(t_rs) > 1.96)
}

Activity 💡

Run sim_slopes() 100 times. How often does each model call the interaction “significant”? How often should it, and why does the model without the random slope do so badly?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
set.seed(707)
purrr::map(1:100, \(i) sim_slopes()) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind() %>%
  dplyr::summarize(intercept_only = mean(intercept_only), random_slope = mean(random_slope))

It should be about 5%. The random-slope model is close to that; the intercept-only model calls the interaction significant far more often. Without the random slope, the model assumes the lame-duck effect is the same in every country, so the country-to-country differences have nowhere to go: the model reads them as evidence about polarization, and counts thousands of rows instead of 12 countries. In a cross-level interaction, a random slope for the lower-level variable might make sense as a default (Heisig & Schaeffer 2019).

Wrap-up 🎁

  • The error term has parts. Comparing different units in the same week cancels the week, \(\theta_t\); comparing a unit with itself cancels its stable traits, \(\nu_i\). Neither alone gets the lame-duck effect right.
  • Nested data make observations alike (the ICC). Ignoring it makes standard errors too small, most of all for group-level variables: cluster at the level where the variable or the treatment varies.
  • Unit fixed effects remove every stable trait, measured or not, and every stable variable with it. Time fixed effects remove shared shocks. Together, they are the difference in differences: the 2×2 table, done for every unit and week.
  • Partial pooling shrinks rarely seen units toward the mean. A plain random-effects model blends within and between; the within-between and bias-corrected models separate them and recover the fixed-effects answer, while still allowing stable variables and predictions for whom.
  • Optional Part IV: a cross-level interaction without a random slope finds effects that are not there.
  • R tools from today: dplyr::mutate(.by = ), estimatr::lm_robust(clusters = ), fixest::feols() with | legislator + week and cluster =, lme4::lmer() with (1 | legislator) and (1 | country/party/legislator), clubSandwich::vcovCR(), re.form = NA, and modelsummary::modelsummary() for side-by-side tables.
